remaining_concerns: No genuinely new admissible evidence was provided; the Actor only narrowed and reframed the same record.
The policy predicate is not just unresolved risk, but material unresolved risk, and materiality is still not established from the admissible record summary alone.
The cited facts more directly support follow-up or escalation than a reject-level decision.
Evidence access is limited to the Actor summary, so the exact contents, context, and admissibility of BPROC-041-C, BPROC-041-D, and BPROC-041-E cannot be independently verified.
The Actor correctly disclaimed any proven control failure, but that caveat does not cure the remaining gap on whether rejection, rather than conditional approval or escalation, was policy-supported.
final_rationale: The verdict does not change. No new admissible evidence was received, and the Actor's response is a reinterpretation of the same evidence already considered. That reinterpretation is narrower and more policy-disciplined: it avoids overstating the record as a proven control failure and limits the theory to unresolved due-diligence risk at decision time. That improves the framing, but it does not resolve the core compliance issue. Under the stated policy, vendor rejection requires admissible due-diligence evidence of a material unresolved risk. On the available summary, the evidence shows a storage-control inconsistency, an informal undocumented quality process, and a procurement note calling for follow-up before approval if storage controls remained unresolved. Those points can support concern, follow-up, or escalation, but they still do not clearly establish that the rejection threshold was met. This is the key distinction: a caveat can narrow an overbroad merits claim, but it is not enough when the caveat leaves an essential compliance predicate unresolved. Business-cost arguments are not evidence and do not affect the audit outcome.
